domain_entities.name: LeaveRequest
attributes: reversesRequestId: string | null  // NEW: null for an original request; the original request's id for a reversal row
domain_entities.purpose: A single application by an employee for a span of leave of one type. Under GP-008 a completed approval is immutable, so a cancellation of an APPROVED request is represented by a SECOND LeaveRequest row (status CANCELLED, reversesRequestId = original.id) rather than by mutating the approved row. The row is therefore either an original request or a reversal of one; both are the same entity type.

domain_entities.name: LeaveRequestEffectiveState
attributes: requestId: string  // the original request id
reversalRequestId: string | null  // the CANCELLED row that reverses it, null when not reversed
domain_entities.purpose: Derived (never persisted) domain value object that collapses the two-row representation of a reversed leave back into one effective state per leave. A leave whose APPROVED row has a reversal child is REVERSED even though that row's persisted status remains APPROVED. This is the concept a client or report uses to answer "what happened to this leave?" without joining rows itself.

domain_entities.name: LeaveBalance
domain_entities.purpose: Per-employee, per-leave-type, per-accrual-period reservation counters. Unchanged by this feature except that the reversal path must release the original reservation exactly once, against the period that holds it.

domain_entities.name: AuditLog
domain_entities.purpose: Immutable record of a state-changing operation (GP-002). A reversal writes exactly one CANCEL entry whose entityId is the NEW reversal row and whose beforeState is the untouched APPROVED original, so the audit trail shows the immutability rather than hiding it.

domain_entities.name: Notification
domain_entities.purpose: Synchronous notification to the affected employee. Unchanged by this feature: a reversal notifies the ORIGINAL request's employeeId, exactly once, in the same transaction as the reversal insert.

business_rules: requestedDays = endDate - startDate + 1 (inclusive calendar days, whole-day UTC, no weekend/holiday exclusion) is the single canonical day-count derivation, implemented once in src/shared/types/index.ts and never re-derived. Every consumer of a day count — the create path, the sufficiency check, the pendingDays reservation on submit, the pendingDays/usedDays release on cancel, and the reversal row's requestedDays — must use this one helper. A reversal row copies the original's requestedDays verbatim rather than recomputing it, so the released amount is provably the reserved amount. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever requestedDays / day-count derivation (create, sufficiency, reservation, release, reversal) appears, not only here]

GP-008 immutability: once a LeaveRequest reaches APPROVED, its status, approverId, approvalComment and decidedAt are immutable. No operation may UPDATE those fields on an APPROVED row. A reversal must not issue any UPDATE against the original row at all. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever LeaveRequest APPROVED rows (all operations) appears, not only here]

Cancelling a DRAFT or SUBMITTED request is an in-place transition of that same row to CANCELLED (no completed approval exists, so GP-008 does not apply). Cancelling an APPROVED request is NOT an in-place transition: it inserts a NEW LeaveRequest row with status CANCELLED and reversesRequestId = original.id, and leaves the original row byte-identical. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever cancel / reversal transition appears, not only here]

A reversal row is a complete LeaveRequest, not a stub: it carries the original's employeeId, leaveTypeCode, startDate, endDate and requestedDays, status CANCELLED, cancelledBy = actor.id, cancelledAt = now, and reversesRequestId = original.id. Its approverId, approvalComment, submittedAt and decidedAt are null — the reversal was never approved, and copying the original's approverId would falsely attribute a decision to the reversal.

The balance release happens exactly once per reversal, in the same transaction as the reversal insert, and is keyed off the ORIGINAL request's status: APPROVED releases requestedDays from usedDays; SUBMITTED releases requestedDays from pendingDays; DRAFT releases nothing. The reversal row itself (status CANCELLED) must never trigger a second release — a CANCELLED row reserves nothing and releases nothing. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever balance release on cancel/reversal appears, not only here]

The balance row released is the one for the accrual period containing the ORIGINAL request's startDate (resolved via periodContaining anchored on the employee's hireDate), read with a row lock before the write. The reversal row's own startDate is identical to the original's, so both resolve to the same period; the release must not be applied to any other period.

A reversal is atomic: the reversal-row insert, the balance release, the CANCEL audit record and the notification all occur inside one unit of work. If any step fails, none of them persist — the original APPROVED row is untouched either way.

A reversal writes exactly one AuditLog entry with action CANCEL, entityType 'leave_request', entityId = the NEW reversal row's id, beforeState = the untouched APPROVED original, afterState = the new CANCELLED reversal row. The audit record for an in-place DRAFT/SUBMITTED cancellation keeps its existing shape (entityId = that row's id).
A reversal notifies the ORIGINAL request's employeeId exactly once, in the same transaction, with relatedEntityId = the reversal row's id. No notification is sent to the actor.

At most one reversal may exist per original request. A request that already has a reversal child (a row whose reversesRequestId = its id) cannot be reversed again; a second attempt is a ConflictError. A reversal row itself (reversesRequestId != null) can never be cancelled or reversed — it is already terminal. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever reversal cardinality / terminality appears, not only here]

Authorization and the timing guard are unchanged by the reversal split: the owner may cancel their own DRAFT or SUBMITTED request; only the requester's direct manager or an ADMIN may cancel an APPROVED request (no self-cancellation of one's own APPROVED request); and cancellation is blocked once startDate <= today (UTC day comparison), which is what makes the full, non-pro-rated release correct.

The read model must expose reversesRequestId so a client can distinguish the two rows of a reversed leave: the APPROVED original (reversesRequestId null) and the CANCELLED reversal (reversesRequestId = original.id). A client must never infer reversal from status alone, because the original's status deliberately still reads APPROVED. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever LeaveRequest read model / GET /leaves appears, not only here]

Role-scoped visibility applies to reversal rows exactly as to originals: a reversal row's employeeId is the original's employeeId, so EMPLOYEE sees their own reversals, MANAGER sees their own plus direct reports' reversals, ADMIN sees all. A reversal row is never hidden from a viewer who can see its original.
domain_notes:
## GP-008 reversal — domain slice

### Entities
- **LeaveRequest** (extended): gains `reversesRequestId: string | null`. Null = an original request; non-null = a reversal row pointing at the original it reverses. All 14 existing fields keep their names, types and nullability. Lifecycle states: DRAFT, SUBMITTED, APPROVED, REJECTED, CANCELLED (unchanged set — no new persisted status is introduced).
- **LeaveRequestEffectiveState** (NEW, derived, never persisted): collapses the two-row representation back to one state per leave. Lifecycle states: DRAFT, SUBMITTED, APPROVED, **REVERSED**, REJECTED, CANCELLED. `REVERSED` is the only NEW lifecycle state this feature introduces, and it is a *derived* state: an APPROVED row with a reversal child reads APPROVED in the database but REVERSED as a leave. It must be folded into architectureMdUpdate alongside the persisted states so no reader mistakes the persisted APPROVED for "still in force".
- **LeaveBalance**: unchanged (OPEN, CLOSED). The reversal path releases against the period containing the original's startDate.
- **AuditLog**: unchanged (RECORDED). One CANCEL entry per reversal, entityId = the new reversal row.
- **Notification**: unchanged (PENDING, SENT, READ, ARCHIVED). One notification per reversal, to the original's employeeId.

### The core domain decision
GP-008 makes a completed approval immutable. The domain therefore splits the single `cancel` operation into two distinct transitions by the original's status:
- **In-place cancellation** (DRAFT, SUBMITTED): the same row moves to CANCELLED. No completed approval exists, so GP-008 does not apply. Unchanged behaviour.
- **Reversal** (APPROVED): the original row is not touched at all — no UPDATE is issued against it. A NEW LeaveRequest row is inserted with status CANCELLED and `reversesRequestId = original.id`. The original's status, approverId, approvalComment and decidedAt remain byte-identical.

The reversal row is a complete LeaveRequest (copies employeeId, leaveTypeCode, startDate, endDate, requestedDays from the original) with approverId/approvalComment/submittedAt/decidedAt null — copying the original's approverId would falsely attribute a decision to a row that was never approved.

### Balance release (must not change)
Release is keyed off the ORIGINAL's status, happens exactly once, in the same transaction as the reversal insert: APPROVED → `usedDays -= requestedDays`; SUBMITTED → `pendingDays -= requestedDays`; DRAFT → nothing. The reversal row (CANCELLED) reserves and releases nothing, so it can never trigger a second release. The balance row is the one for the accrual period containing the original's startDate, read with a row lock before the write. The full, non-pro-rated release stays correct because the existing timing guard blocks cancellation once `startDate <= today`.

### Cardinality and terminality
At most one reversal per original (a second attempt is a ConflictError). A reversal row is terminal: it can never be cancelled or reversed again.

### Read model
`reversesRequestId` must be exposed on the read model so a client can tell the two rows apart. A client must never infer reversal from status alone — the original deliberately still reads APPROVED. Role-scoped visibility applies to reversal rows exactly as to originals (same employeeId).

### Audit and notification
One CANCEL AuditLog entry per reversal: entityId = the NEW reversal row's id, beforeState = the untouched APPROVED original, afterState = the new CANCELLED reversal row. One notification to the original's employeeId, relatedEntityId = the reversal row's id. Both inside the single unit of work with the insert and the release.

### Open questions raised
1. Whether GET /leaves returns both rows or collapses to one effective entry.
2. Whether the reversal row copies the original's date span (double-count risk in date-range queries) or nulls it.
3. Whether a reversal needs a human reason field, and where it lives.

### Persistence / API notes (for the data and application architects, not decided here)
The data architect owns the `reverses_request_id` column, its index, the FK to `leave_requests.id`, and the knex migration; the application architect owns the `cancel` branch, the read-model projection and the wire contract. This slice fixes only the domain semantics above.

open_questions.question: Should GET /leaves return reversal rows by default, or should the read model collapse a reversed leave into a single entry (the original, with effectiveState REVERSED)?
open_questions.impact: A reversed leave now occupies two rows. Returning both is honest but doubles the row count for a single leave and makes naive client counts (e.g. "how many approved leaves") wrong unless the client filters on reversesRequestId. Collapsing server-side hides the reversal row's id from clients that want to link to it. This affects every list consumer (web LeaveListPage, approvals queue, dashboard counts) and the smoke assertions.
candidate_options: Return both rows unchanged; clients distinguish via reversesRequestId (current spec reading)
Return both rows but add a derived effectiveState field so clients need not join
Return only the original row, with effectiveState REVERSED and reversalRequestId set; hide the reversal row from lists but keep it reachable by GET /leaves/:id

open_questions.question: Should a reversal row carry the original's startDate/endDate (making it match date-range and leaveTypeCode list filters), or should those span fields be null on a reversal since a reversal is not itself a leave span?
open_questions.impact: Copying the span keeps the reversal row self-describing and lets a client render it without a join, but it means a date-range query for a period returns both the original and its reversal, and any consumer summing requestedDays over a date range double-counts unless it filters reversesRequestId. Nulling the span avoids the double-count but breaks the "reversal row is a complete LeaveRequest" shape and any NOT NULL constraint on start_date/end_date.
candidate_options: Copy startDate/endDate/requestedDays from the original (current spec reading); consumers must filter reversesRequestId to avoid double-counting
Copy startDate/endDate but set requestedDays = 0 on the reversal row
Null startDate/endDate/requestedDays on the reversal row and relax the NOT NULL constraints

open_questions.question: Should a reversal row record a reason/comment explaining why the approved leave was reversed, and if so in which field?
open_questions.impact: The current cancel operation accepts no body, so a reversal carries no human explanation; the audit log's beforeState/afterState plus cancelledBy is the only trace. If reversals of approved leave need an explanation for compliance, the wire contract (POST /leaves/:id/cancel body) and the reversal row's fields both change, and approvalComment cannot be reused because it is reserved for the approval decision.
candidate_options: No reason field; cancelledBy + cancelledAt + audit log are sufficient
Reuse the existing reason field on the reversal row for the reversal rationale
Add a dedicated reversalReason field and accept an optional body on the cancel endpoint
